newsitem.title: USA: Mass. abolishes Middlesex County, Harvard's home.
newsitem.headline: Mass. abolishes Middlesex County, Harvard's home.

text.p: Massachusetts Gov. William Weld signed Friday a bill abolishing Middlesex County, a move he described as the first step in eliminating an inefficient holdover from the state's colonial government.

"Over the last three centuries, counties have become obsolete, inward-looking bureaucracies, with dozens of departments and department heads that serve themselves and not the taxpayer," Weld said in prepared remarks.

"The legislation that we are signing today is a good first step in eliminating a vestige of Massachusetts colonial government." Weld has tried to end all counties, saying he could run them more efficiently at a lower cost. He plans to file a new bill to kill them off by July 1, 1999. Recently, the state has bailed out three or four counties a year.
Middlesex, home of Harvard University and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, runs north from Cambridge to the New Hampshire border and west to Framingham.

All the essential functions and property of Middlesex County, including jails and courts, will be transferred to the state immediately. Massachusetts takes over all the county's assets and liabilities, with the registry of deeds becoming part of the Secretary of State's office. A Massachusetts Representative who wrote that house's bill abolishing the county has said the Registry produces $25 million of fees.

Two other counties, Worchester, in central Massachusetts, and Hampdon, which includes Springfield, in the western part of the state, also will be transferred to the state by July 1, 1998, or sooner if they default on a debt payment.

Middlesex's problems moved to the front burner late last year, after it defaulted on $4.7 million of revenue anticipation notes. The Middlesex County Retirement system has an unfunded pension liability of over $235 million, of which the county's share is $38.7 million, according to a 1996 Coopers & Lybrand estimate. The rest of the obligation is shared by the 64 municipalities that are part of the system.
